title: Osteoporosis Self évaluation Tool (OST)
formula: OST = (weight, kg - age, years) * 0.2, truncated to an integer

how_to_use.why:
- Its simplicity makes it an effective bedside tool.
- Helps avoid unnecessary BMD testing in patients at low risk of osteoporosis.
how_to_use.when:
- Can be used during routine health visits in the outpatient setting to assess the risk of low bone mineral density (BMD) and determine which patients may benefit from bone densitometry.
- Particularly beneficial in resource-limited settings, assessing men, and evaluating women under 65 years of age, where decisions to pursue BMD testing are based on specific clinical factors.
how_to_use.pearls:
- Validated for use in men and women aged 40 years and older.
- Comparable in performance to other osteoporosis risk assessment tools.
- Does not account for all osteoporosis risk factors and should not replace clinical judgment.
- Not intended as a diagnostic tool. Results should prompt further evaluation, where appropriate.
- Several studies have used different cutoffs when determining risk levels. This particular tool uses cutoffs provided by the original derivation study for women ([Koh, 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11580084/)) and a validation study for men ([Adler, 2003](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12934782/)).

next_steps.management:
- Low risk: Bone densitometry testing may be postponed or avoided; focus on lifestyle modifications and routine monitoring.
- Intermediate and high risk: Bone densitometry should be considered to confirm risk and guide the initiation of appropriate management strategies, including pharmacologic interventions if indicated.

more_info:
Interpretation for women:

| OST Index | Osteoporosis Risk |
| --- | --- |
| >1 | Low |
| -3 to 1 | Intermediate |
| < -3 | High |

Interpretation for men:

| OST Index | Osteoporosis Risk |
| --- | --- |
| >3 | Low |
| -1 to 3 | Intermediate |
| <-1 | High |

Several studies have used different cutoffs when determining risk levels. This particular tool uses cutoffs provided by the original derivation study for women ([Koh, 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11580084/)) and a validation study for men ([Adler, 2003](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12934782/)).
